title: Lesson 2: Auditing How You Actually Work: Finding the Repetitive 20 Percent
description: The audit method for finding the repetitive slice of your work: listing recurring tasks, measuring their effort, and flagging the same-shaped ones that are the best first candidates for a workflow.

questions.question: A time audit exists to correct which specific bias in how people plan their own work?
options: People underestimate how long a single large task takes to finish
Memory inflates urgent work and hides the quiet, repetitive kind
People assume that every task they do can be automated with a tool
People overestimate how much of their week is spent in meetings
questions.explanation: Memory records what was vivid, not what consumed the most time, so it inflates urgent or interesting work and hides the routine tasks that quietly fill the week.

questions.question: A task done ten minutes every day and a task done two hours once a month both appear on an audit. Which consumes more time, and why?
options: The monthly task, because a single long session costs more than a short one
The monthly task, because infrequent work tends to be more demanding
The daily task, because frequency times duration beats a rare long block
They consume the same, because both average out over a month
questions.explanation: Total effort is frequency times duration. A small daily task adds up to more than a large monthly one, which is why an audit ranks by measured total rather than by how big a task feels.

questions.question: Which task belongs in the first set you automate?
options: One with the same inputs, steps, and output format on every run
One you run a few times a year but that carries high stakes
One that requires fresh judgment about what to include each time
One that depends on other people sending you material first
questions.explanation: A strong first candidate is frequent, same-shaped, and low-risk to get wrong. Work that shifts shape or needs fresh judgment has no stable frame for a saved flow to run.
